short: Passed following the execution of Anne Boleyn, this Act declared both Mary and Elizabeth illegitimate and allowed Henry VIII to designate his heir.
full:
Enacted in July 1536, weeks after Anne Boleyn's execution and Henry VIII's marriage to Jane Seymour, the Second Succession Act comprehensively rearranged the line to the throne. It declared Henry's marriage to Anne null and void, legally bastardising their daughter, Princess Elizabeth. Combined with the first act's treatment of Princess Mary, Henry was left with no legitimate children to inherit the crown.

To address this unprecedented crisis, Parliament granted the King an extraordinary power: the right to determine the succession by letters patent or by his last will and testament, bypassing customary inheritance laws entirely. This allowed him to potentially elevate his illegitimate son, Henry FitzRoy, or any other chosen successor. The Act remained in force until FitzRoy's death and the birth of Prince Edward in 1537 reshaped the dynastic landscape once again.
